roadmap.goal: The on-premise Jira instance the epic was written about gets delta refreshes. `SupportsIncrementalSync` starts answering yes for Data Center as well as Cloud, and the identity sweep learns Data Center's own transport - an offset walk over `rest/api/latest/search` asking for `key,updated` and nothing else, with no changelog - because Data Center has neither Cloud's `search/jql` endpoint nor its page token. The sweep appends its own `ORDER BY key ASC`, replacing whatever ordering the operator's own query carries, so that an edit during an eight-second walk cannot move a record onto a page already read and out of `removed = stored - swept`. Both by-reference-id fetches answer to the same capability, so a connector that cannot sweep is never asked to fetch by key. One sweep contract across both deployments - a connector implements a sweep, it does not choose a strategy.
absorbed_steps: The capability flip and the Data Center walk are ONE step (01-02) rather than two, and this is the roadmap's single largest sequencing decision. `SweepIdentities` refuses before it walks, so no sweep specification can go red for the right reason while `SupportsIncrementalSync` answers no for Data Center - every one of them lands on `NotSupportedException: Only Jira Cloud sweeps` from `SweepIdentities:95`, which is MISSING_FUNCTIONALITY and correct but proves nothing about the specification's own assertions. The moment the capability answers yes, the four shipped `..._RefusesOnDataCenter` tests and `SupportsIncrementalSync_StaysFalseForDataCenter` all turn red at once, verified by DISTILL rather than predicted: a throwaway probe widening the capability to `deployment != Unknown` reddened all five with `Expected: <NotSupportedException> But was: no exception thrown`. Those five must be deleted in the same step that un-ignores their replacements, so the replacements for all five - specifications 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 - land here too. It is the deletions that set this step's size, not the implementation: 10, 11 and 12 come free with the flip and are un-ignored because their opposite numbers cannot survive it. Everything the flip does not force is deliberately left for its own commit: the sweep's narrowing (02-01), what it reports per record (02-02), its refusal to half-answer (02-03) and its ordering (03-01, 03-02).

steps.implementation_notes: AC-4.4 / AC-4.5, contract shape `bounded-change`. EXPECT BOTH GREEN ON ARRIVAL and record the run rather than inventing work; the connector file is listed as where a fix would land. Specification 3 is forced by the stub before it is asserted - 01-02 could not have satisfied specification 2's offset assertion without naming `fields=key,updated`, because that is what the stub's sweep branch keys on (`JiraIncrementalSyncTest.cs:966`). steps.implementation_notes: AC-4.4, contract shape `bounded-change`. BOTH SHOULD BE GREEN if 01-02 read its stamps through the shared `ReadStamp` (`JiraWorkTrackingConnector.cs:132`); if specification 8 reds here, the Data Center walk grew its own parse and the fix is to DELETE that parse rather than to correct it. WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS (D12): the swept stamp is compared against the stored stamp per record with no watermark in between, so two different readings of one string report every record as moved, forever - a delta that downloads everything, every cycle, with every test green. `ReadStamp` parses the way `IssueFactory` parses, which is what makes the two halves comparable at all. SPECIFICATION 9 IS THE ONE THAT CHANGED CLASS between DISTILL's two probe runs: under the naive probe it failed with `Expected: default But was: 2026-08-01 10:00:00`, and the reason is worth knowing before you read a failure here - the sweep never reached the Data Center path at all, so the stub answered with the canned Cloud issue rather than from `OffsetSweepIssues`. With the offset walk in place it should read the seeded record and find no `updated` field. If it fails the same way now, the walk is not reading the offset pager. WHAT IT PROTECTS: leaving an unstamped record out of the sweep puts it in `stored minus swept` and DELETES A LIVE ITEM, where reporting it with no stamp merely re-downloads it - no stamp can never equal a stored stamp. Ambiguity resolving to the expensive answer is the same rule D8 applies everywhere else in this epic. PROVE BOTH CAN FAIL: for 8, temporarily parse the stamp with a different set of `DateTimeStyles` (dropping `AdjustToUniversal` is enough, and it is also the realistic mistake) and confirm it reds; for 9, temporarily filter records with no readable stamp out of the swept list and confirm the first assertion reds. Revert both, confirm `git status --porcelain` is clean of production edits. Preflight and gates as in 01-01.

criteria: A Data Center sweep whose second page is rejected refuses to answer, with the same kind of failure the Cloud sweep raises for the same situation, naming what was being swept
The refusal is distinguishable from the refusal a connector gives when it cannot sweep at all - a sweep that never walked a page cannot satisfy this specification
The first page having been read successfully before the rejection is what the specification exercises, and the walk is verified to have reached the second offset
The specification runs un-ignored in this commit, and the full backend suite is green with zero build warnings
steps.implementation_notes: AC-4.2 / AC-4.4, contract shape `unbounded-preservation` - it claims an absence, that no half-walked answer ever reaches the caller. THIS IS THE ONE SPECIFICATION IN THE SET DISTILL'S NAIVE PROBE REDDENED OUTRIGHT (`Expected: <InvalidOperationException> But was: no exception thrown`), and it is also the one the RED gate caught as a wrong-reason green and re-shaped: it first shipped asserting `Throws.Exception` and PASSED ON ARRIVAL, satisfied by the `Only Jira Cloud sweeps` refusal without a single page ever being walked. It would have gone green at DELIVER the moment the capability lifted, while the half-walk protection it is named after was never exercised. It now asserts `Throws.TypeOf<InvalidOperationException>()`, which a `NotSupportedException` cannot satisfy. DO NOT WEAKEN IT BACK. THE SHAPE: the Cloud path answers a rejected page by returning false from its walk and letting `SweepIdentities` throw `InvalidOperationException` naming the swept description (`JiraWorkTrackingConnector.cs:116-119`). The Data Center walk needs the same shape. DO NOT reach for `EnsureSuccessStatusCode()` the way `GetIssuesByQueryFromDataCenter` does - that throws `HttpRequestException` and the specification is typed. READ THE STUB'S COUNTER BEFORE YOU DEBUG A SURPRISE: `FailTheSearchAfterTheNextOne` sets the failure to begin at `searchCount + 2`, and the fixture helper has already issued one full-fetch search, so the sweep's FIRST page succeeds and its SECOND is answered with 500. That is precisely the half-walk this exists for - one page read, one page lost - so a walk that fails before reading anything, or one that swallows the 500 and returns what it has, are both wrong for different reasons. WHY IT IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: removal is `stored minus swept`. Returning the first offset as if it were the whole query deletes every record on the pages that never arrived, and on this instance that is decades of work. Throwing falls back to a full fetch, which is slow and correct. PROVE IT CAN FAIL: temporarily return the stamps collected so far instead of refusing, confirm it reds, revert. Preflight and gates as in 01-01.

phases.name: An order no edit can disturb
phases.description: AC-4.2's other half, and the only part of the slice that was not settled by the 2026-08-11 probe. The probe returned a stable id set over three passes of 5056 issues, but each walk took about eight seconds against a quiet instance, so it could not exercise an edit landing mid-walk. Offset paging asks for `issues 500 to 549 of the current answer`; an edit reshuffles Jira's default relevance ordering and can move a record onto a page already read, so it never appears in the sweep and `stored minus swept` deletes it. That residual is closed by construction rather than by measurement: an ordering on the key cannot be disturbed by an edit, because an issue's key never changes. Two steps, not one, and the split is load-bearing - an unconditional append satisfies the first and is exactly what the second forbids.

steps.implementation_notes: AC-4.2, contract shape `bounded-change`. THE ORDERING IS DATA-CENTER-ONLY AND SWEEP-ONLY, and both halves of that are enforced by tests you can red by accident. Sweep-only: the whole download keeps its ordering, because Jira's rank field drives item order in Lighthouse and rewriting the download's ordering would quietly change what manual sorting shows users - see `out_of_scope`. Data-Center-only, and this is the one a reasonable implementation gets wrong by generalising: the SHIPPED CLOUD sweep tests compare the sweep's JQL to the full fetch's by EXACT equality with no allowance for an ordering clause - `SweepWorkItemsForTeam_AsksTheVeryQuestionTheWholeQueryAsks` (`JiraIncrementalSyncTest.cs:135`) and `SweepParentFeatures_SweepsTheSameKeyedQueryTheParentDetailFetchIssues` (`:504`) - while every Data Center specification strips the ordering first with the fixture's own `WithoutOrdering` helper (`:809`). So an ordering applied inside the shared sweep entry point reds shipped Cloud tests, and an ordering applied on the Data Center branch does not. That asymmetry is correct and is the reason this is a transport decision rather than a sweep-contract decision: Cloud's walk is token-paged, and a page token is not an offset into a re-sorted answer, so Cloud has no exposure to the hazard this closes. RE-RUN SPECIFICATIONS 4 AND 11 IN THIS COMMIT (`SweepWorkItemsForTeam_OnDataCenter_EnumeratesTheSameQueryTheWholeDownloadEnumerates`, `SweepParentFeatures_OnDataCenter_SweepsTheSameKeyedQueryTheParentDetailFetchIssues`). Both compare the sweep's query to the download's after stripping the ordering; if either reds here, the ordering changed WHAT is enumerated rather than in what order, which is the failure that turns `stored minus swept` into a deletion. NOTE ON THE KEYED SWEEP: `SweepParentFeatures` sweeps a `key = "X" OR key = "Y"` query, which takes an ordering clause perfectly well, so no special case is needed there - and specification 11's `WithoutOrdering` is what lets it keep comparing. WHY ASSERT RATHER THAN MEASURE: the probe ran clean, and the slice brief says so; it also says why that is not enough - the instance was quiet and each walk took about eight seconds, so churn during a walk was never exercised. An ordering on an immutable field cannot be disturbed by an edit, which the default relevance ordering cannot promise. That is the whole argument, and it is why AC-4.2 is closed by construction. AN UNCONDITIONAL APPEND IS THE RIGHT IMPLEMENTATION FOR THIS STEP. 03-02 is what turns it into a replacement, and it is a separate commit precisely so that red is not spent here. Preflight and gates as in 01-01.

steps.implementation_notes: AC-4.2, contract shape `bounded-change`. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN STEP: after 03-01's unconditional append, this specification's FIRST assertion - exactly one ordering clause - is the honest red, and DISTILL's naive-probe run recorded exactly that shape (`its first assertion passes here, which is what a naive append would break`). Two `ORDER BY` clauses is not valid JQL, so a naive append breaks the sweep for precisely the operators who write their own JQL, which is who runs this deployment. Merging 03-01 and 03-02 would spend this red. THE TRAP, AND THE SPECIFICATION CANNOT SEE IT. `PrepareQuery` (`JiraWorkTrackingConnector.cs:1541`) wraps the operator's `DataRetrievalValue` in parentheses - `({query}) {types} {states} {cutoff}` - so for `project = PROJ ORDER BY created DESC` the string the sweep receives is `(project = PROJ ORDER BY created DESC) AND (issuetype = "Story") ...`, with the operator's ordering INSIDE the parentheses and not at the tail. Truncating the whole JQL at the first `ORDER BY` therefore leaves `(project = PROJ`, which is unbalanced garbage - and the specification would still PASS, because `OrderingClausesIn` (`:816`) only counts occurrences and the second assertion only checks the tail. So this is one the crafter has to get right without the test as judge: strip the ordering from the operator's own query value while it is still a standalone expression, before it is parenthesised, then append the sweep's ordering to the finished JQL. The specification prints the query it got (`Asked for: {jql}`) - read it, and read the one 03-01's team produces too. RECORDED AND OUT OF SCOPE: the FULL FETCH's handling of the same query is already broken today, for Cloud as much as for Data Center, because `PrepareQuery` parenthesises it there too. Specification 6 covers the sweep because the sweep is what this slice adds. Do not fix the full fetch here; flag it as its own ADO item. PROVE IT CAN FAIL: revert to the unconditional append, confirm the clause-count assertion reds and specification 5 stays green, then restore. Preflight and gates as in 01-01.
